questions.stem: A people-operations coordinator gets about a dozen questions a week from managers about the company's own parental-leave and remote-work policies. She wants Claude to help her draft accurate answers quickly. The policies live in a 40-page internal handbook that changes once or twice a year. Which approach is the MOST appropriate starting point?

options.text: Turn on Research for each question so Claude searches widely across public web sources and returns a cited answer.
Create a Project holding the current handbook, with instructions to answer from it and cite the section used.
Start a fresh chat each time, relying on Claude's general knowledge of typical parental-leave and remote policies.
Ask Claude to summarize the handbook once, then paste that short summary into every new conversation.

questions.explanation: The answers must come from **the company's own handbook**, not the open web or general knowledge. A **Project** keeps the handbook as a knowledge source and holds standing instructions, so every new chat starts grounded in the right document. Asking Claude to name the applicable section also makes each draft quick to check before she replies to a manager.

whyWrong.A: Research is built for multi-source web investigation. Public web pages describe other companies' policies, not hers, so the citations would point at the wrong source of truth.
whyWrong.C: General knowledge describes typical parental-leave and remote-work policies, which may differ from her company's. Drafts would sound right and be wrong in the details that matter.
whyWrong.D: A pasted summary drops the detail (eligibility rules, exceptions) that manager questions hinge on, and repasting it into every conversation is the manual work a Project removes.

questions.mindset: Match the feature to where the truth lives: internal documents belong in a Project, not a web search.

questions.stem: A product marketer plans to use Research to investigate how small accounting firms choose practice-management software. The findings will shape next quarter's messaging. Her draft prompt is simply: 'Research accounting software buying behavior.' Which TWO additions would MOST improve the usefulness and reliability of the report? Choose TWO.

options.text: State the decision the report must support and the topics a useful answer covers, such as buying triggers and sign-off.
Add an instruction telling Claude to be completely accurate and to leave out any information that might be wrong.
Ask Claude to consult as many sources as it can find, so the volume of citations makes the report more convincing.
Set a date window and source preferences, and ask Claude to flag every finding that rests on a single source.
Switch to the largest available model before starting, since a bigger model will simply infer the scope she has in mind.

questions.explanation: A one-line prompt leaves Claude to guess the scope. The core prompting guidance is to **be clear and direct**: state what the output is for and what a useful answer must cover (A). And because confident-but-unsupported claims are a known failure mode, verification has to be built into the task: narrowing the time window and source types and asking which findings rest on a single source (D) separates well-supported findings from weak ones and tells the marketer exactly what to double-check before the report shapes next quarter's messaging.

whyWrong.B: Telling a model to 'never be wrong' gives it no new information or method. It is wishful phrasing, not a control; the real safeguards are scoping plus human checking of key claims.
whyWrong.C: More sources is not better sources. A pile of weak citations looks convincing while making the report harder to verify.
whyWrong.E: No model can infer a scope the prompt never states. The gap is missing criteria, not model size.

questions.mindset: A research prompt needs a goal, a scope and a way to tell strong findings from weak ones.

questions.stem: A strategy analyst asks Claude, using Research, to estimate the size of the regional market for refurbished medical equipment. The cited report quotes three sources whose figures differ by almost a factor of two. The analyst must give the finance director one number to use in a business case next week. What is the BEST next step?

options.text: Use the figure in the middle of the three, since averaging the sources cancels out each one's individual errors.
Run Research again with the same prompt and use whichever of the figures appears most often across the two reports.
Have Claude set out each figure with its source and definition, check the originals, and present a reasoned range.
Use the highest figure, since it comes from the most recent source and markets of this kind generally keep growing.

questions.explanation: Big gaps between sources usually come from **different definitions, dates or methods** (one counts only hospitals, another includes clinics). Claude can lay out those differences fast; the analyst then opens the originals to confirm them. A range with stated assumptions is honest and defensible in a business case. Citations are a starting point to check, not proof that the numbers agree.

whyWrong.A: Averaging figures that measure different things produces a number nobody published and nobody can defend when finance asks where it came from.
whyWrong.B: Rerunning may surface the same sources again. Frequency across runs doesn't resolve why the figures differ, and it verifies nothing.
whyWrong.D: Picking the highest figure on an assumption of growth is a convenient guess. Newer isn't automatically comparable, and the choice biases the business case.

questions.mindset: When sources disagree, explain the disagreement and verify; don't average or guess it away.

questions.stem: A sales-operations lead has started using Research for nearly everything, including questions like 'what does EBITDA stand for' and 'reformat this table'. By midweek he keeps hitting his usage limit and can't run the deeper competitor investigations his manager actually needs. What change would MOST effectively solve this?

options.text: Upgrade every member of the team to the highest plan so that his habits no longer run into the usage limits.
Stop using Research altogether and do the competitor investigations by hand, so the limits are never reached.
Put all of the quick questions into one very long conversation so they share a single Research session.
Use ordinary chat for quick questions and edits, and reserve Research for multi-source investigations needing citations.

questions.explanation: Research runs many searches and builds a long, cited answer, so it is the heaviest way to answer a question in chat. Quick definitions and formatting jobs never needed it. Matching the feature to the depth of the question — ordinary chat for quick items, Research for multi-source investigation — frees capacity for the competitor work his manager actually needs.

whyWrong.A: Spending more to accommodate a wasteful habit treats the symptom. The mismatch between task and feature remains.
whyWrong.B: Abandoning the feature throws away its real value for multi-source work, when a simple change in habits fixes the problem.
whyWrong.C: A single sprawling conversation is itself heavy to process, and the quick questions still never needed Research in the first place.

questions.mindset: Use the lightest tool that answers the question; save the heavy one for heavy questions.

questions.stem: A project coordinator asks Claude to draft a 10-week rollout plan for a new expense tool across four offices. The plan looks polished, but she notices it assumes two-day training sessions, an IT security review of three days and no holiday periods, none of which she supplied. She must share the plan with office heads tomorrow. What should she do FIRST?

options.text: Ask Claude to list every assumption behind the plan, then confirm the key ones with the people who own those steps.
Share the plan as written but add a footnote saying it was produced by AI and that some dates might change later.
Ask Claude to regenerate the plan several times and keep the version whose timeline looks the most realistic overall.
Discard the draft and build the plan manually, since a plan that contains invented details can never be trusted.

questions.explanation: Claude filled gaps with plausible guesses because it wasn't given the real constraints. The fix is to **make the assumptions visible** and **check them with the owners** (IT for the security review, office heads for training and holidays), then feed the confirmed facts back in. The structure of the draft is still useful; only the unverified inputs need work.

whyWrong.B: A disclaimer doesn't fix wrong dates. Office heads will plan around numbers nobody has validated.
whyWrong.C: Every regeneration still rests on guessed constraints. 'Looks realistic' is a feeling, not a check against how long IT actually takes.
whyWrong.D: The draft is a sound starting structure. Throwing it away wastes the useful part when only the assumptions need confirming.

questions.mindset: A plan is only as real as its constraints: surface the assumptions and have owners confirm them.

questions.stem: A facilities manager needs Claude's help planning an office relocation: lease exit, IT cut-over, furniture, staff communications and a weekend move. His first attempt, asking for 'a complete detailed move plan' in one go, produced a very long document that he found hard to check and that mixed up the order of IT tasks. Which approach would MOST likely give him a plan he can trust?

options.text: Ask for the same complete plan again but require twice the detail, so that nothing important gets left out.
Ask Claude to check its own long plan for mistakes and then confirm that the finished document is fully correct.
Agree a phase outline first, then get detail one phase at a time, reviewing each before moving on.
Hand the whole relocation to an autonomous agent that can book vendors and schedule IT work without his input.

questions.explanation: Breaking a big planning job into stages, **outline first, then one phase at a time**, keeps each piece small enough to check. He can fix the IT sequencing in the outline before any detail is built on it, and each phase gets his full attention and the relevant facts. Draft, review against criteria, refine — one step at a time — is the reliable pattern for work like this.

whyWrong.A: A longer version of the same one-shot request is even harder to review and carries the same ordering errors.
whyWrong.B: Self-review can catch some slips, but Claude doesn't know his building, vendors or IT dependencies. A 'fully correct' confirmation from the same model isn't verification.
whyWrong.D: Letting an agent commit vendors and IT work removes his judgment from costly decisions, and building such an agent is technical work to escalate, not an Associate chat task.

questions.mindset: Big plans are checked in pieces: outline, approve, then detail phase by phase.

questions.stem: An insurance claims supervisor pastes the current 14-step claims-intake procedure into Claude and asks how to make it faster. Claude's answer is well reasoned and recommends removing step 9, a second sign-off on claims above a set amount, as 'redundant because step 6 already reviews the claim'. The change would save about a day per large claim. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: Remove step 9 straight away, because the saving is large and Claude's reasoning about the overlap seems clear.
Check with the compliance or risk owner why the second sign-off on larger claims exists before proposing to remove it.
Ask Claude whether it is confident about the recommendation and remove the step if it reports high confidence.
Reject all of Claude's suggestions, since it has proposed removing a control and may have made other errors too.

questions.explanation: Claude can see the steps but not **why** they exist. A second sign-off above a threshold often comes from regulation, audit findings or fraud controls. The supervisor should check with the owner of that control. If it turns out to be historical, removing it is a good win; if it's required, Claude can help find savings elsewhere, for example by preparing the sign-off package faster.

whyWrong.A: Clear reasoning about the document isn't knowledge of the regulatory or fraud reasons behind it. Removing a financial control on that basis is a costly risk.
whyWrong.C: Claude's stated confidence doesn't add information it doesn't have. It can't know the audit history behind the step.
whyWrong.D: One suggestion needing checking doesn't make the rest worthless. The sensible path verifies the risky change and keeps the useful ideas.

questions.mindset: Before cutting a step, learn why it exists; Claude sees the process, not its history.

questions.stem: An accounts-payable team lead has mapped her team's invoice process with Claude's help and is now deciding where Claude should assist. The team works in Claude's chat interface and has no developer support this quarter. Which TWO steps are the BEST candidates for Claude assistance? Choose TWO.

options.text: Approving invoices below a set amount automatically whenever Claude finds that they match a purchase order.
Sorting supplier email queries by topic and drafting replies that an AP clerk reviews and then sends.
Deciding which suppliers to drop from the approved list based on Claude's analysis of late deliveries.
Having Claude post invoice data straight into the finance system from chat to remove manual entry.
Summarizing the payment terms of long supplier contracts for a clerk who checks them against each invoice.

questions.explanation: Strong fits are tasks where **Claude reads or drafts and a person checks**: sorting and drafting replies to supplier queries (B) and summarizing payment terms for a clerk to confirm (E). Both save real time, keep a human on anything that leaves the team or moves money, and need nothing beyond chat.

whyWrong.A: Approving payments is a financial commitment. Removing the human from it, even for small amounts, turns a matching aid into an unreviewed control.
whyWrong.C: Dropping a supplier is a business decision with relationship and contract consequences. Claude can analyze delivery data, but people make the call.
whyWrong.D: Writing into a finance system from chat needs a proper integration with access controls — technical work to escalate to Developers or Architects, not a chat task.

questions.mindset: Give Claude the reading and drafting; keep approvals, commitments and system writes with people and proper builds.

questions.stem: A program manager asks Research to compare industry best practices for vendor onboarding with 'how we currently do it'. The report covers public sources well but ignores the team's current onboarding process, which is documented in a checklist the team maintains in a shared Google Doc. What should she do to get the comparison she wants with the least effort?

options.text: Recreate the onboarding checklist from memory, paste the result into the chat, and run the research again.
Ask Claude to infer the team's current process from typical vendor-onboarding practices and compare against that.
Ask IT to build a custom integration that feeds the team's documents into every future research report automatically.
Copy the checklist steps from the Doc into the request and rerun Research, comparing best practices against them.

questions.explanation: The report missed the internal half because nothing in the request gave Claude the team's actual process. Copying the real checklist steps into the request supplies the authoritative internal source directly, grounding the comparison in how the team actually works. It is also the least-effort path: no rebuilding from memory, no guessed baseline, no new tooling — the discipline of giving Claude the relevant documents rather than letting it fill gaps.

whyWrong.A: Rebuilding from memory can quietly replace the team's real steps with recollections. The authoritative checklist already exists and takes moments to copy.
whyWrong.B: An inferred 'current process' is a plausible fiction. A comparison against a guess tells the team nothing about its own workflow.
whyWrong.C: A custom integration is a disproportionate fix for one report missing one known document, and system integration is technical work to escalate, not a prerequisite for this comparison.

questions.mindset: When research needs your internal reality, hand over the real document instead of letting Claude guess or rebuilding it.

questions.stem: A warehouse supervisor asks Claude in a normal chat, with web search off, to summarize a parcel carrier's new packaging and labelling rules, which the carrier announced last month. Claude gives a confident, detailed answer. The supervisor plans to retrain packing staff on it next week. What should he do?

options.text: Rerun the question with web search on, then check the key rules against the carrier's own published notice.
Use the answer for training, since it is detailed and specific enough to suggest Claude knows about the change.
Ask Claude in the same chat to confirm that its summary reflects last month's rules before using it for training.
Skip Claude for this and wait for the carrier to send printed guidance, since AI can't be used for compliance topics.

questions.explanation: A change from last month may be **after Claude's training data**, and without web search Claude can't look it up. A detailed answer may describe the old rules or fill gaps plausibly. Turning on web search or Research gets current sources, and checking the carrier's own notice confirms the rules before staff are retrained on them.

whyWrong.B: Detail and confidence are not evidence of currency. Hallucinated or outdated answers often sound just as specific.
whyWrong.C: Without web access, Claude can't learn anything new in the same chat. Its confirmation repeats what it already said.
whyWrong.D: Avoiding Claude entirely is unnecessary. With current sources plus a check against the official notice, Claude can save him real time.

questions.mindset: For recent changes, get current sources and confirm against the official one before acting.

questions.stem: A delivery manager uploads 20 sprint-retrospective documents to Claude and asks for the recurring problems slowing the team down. Claude returns six themes. Her director, who will fund fixes based on this, asks how she knows the themes really come from the retros and weren't simply invented. Which approach BEST addresses the director's concern?

options.text: Ask Claude to support each theme with direct quotes and a count of how many retros mention it, then spot-check them.
Ask Claude to restate the six themes in confident, authoritative wording so they read as established findings.
Run the same request through a different AI assistant and present only the themes that both tools happen to list.
Tell the director the themes are reliable because Claude read all 20 documents, which no person had time to do.

questions.explanation: Asking Claude to **ground its answer in quotes** from the documents is a recommended technique for long-document work. Quotes plus a mention count make every theme traceable, and a quick spot-check of a few quotes against the originals gives the director real evidence rather than assurance.

whyWrong.B: Stronger wording makes the themes sound more certain without adding any evidence. It makes the director's concern worse, not better.
whyWrong.C: Agreement between two tools isn't traceability. Both could miss or invent the same plausible-sounding theme, and the director still can't see the source.
whyWrong.D: Breadth of reading isn't proof of accuracy. Without traceable evidence, this asks the director to take the output on trust.

questions.mindset: Make synthesized findings traceable to the source so others can check them.

questions.stem: Five team leads in a customer-success department each use Claude to draft their weekly capacity plan. The head of department finds the plans hard to combine: each uses a different format, some ignore the department's standard working-hours rule, and leads waste time re-explaining context every week. Which change would MOST efficiently fix this?

options.text: Ask each lead to write a longer weekly prompt that restates the format and the working-hours rule every time.
Create a shared Project holding the plan template, the working-hours rule and instructions that all leads follow.
Have the head of department rewrite all five plans into one format by hand each Monday before combining them.
Request a developer-built planning application that generates the plans automatically from the team's ticket data.

questions.explanation: This is recurring work with shared rules and shared reference material — exactly what **Projects** are for. The template, the working-hours rule and the instructions live in one place and apply to every chat in the Project, so all five leads start from the same setup and nobody re-explains context each week.

whyWrong.A: Longer weekly prompts depend on five people remembering the same details every week, which is the inconsistency they already have.
whyWrong.C: This moves the rework onto the head of department instead of preventing it. The process stays inefficient.
whyWrong.D: A custom build is over-engineered for a consistency problem that a shared Project solves today with no development.

questions.mindset: Recurring shared work gets a shared Project, not repeated prompts or manual clean-up.

questions.stem: A customer-onboarding lead has used Claude to redesign her team's onboarding process. Claude's future-state design estimates it will 'cut onboarding time by about 60%'. She has to win approval from the operations director, who is sceptical of AI claims. Which TWO actions would MOST strengthen her proposal? Choose TWO.

options.text: Quote Claude's 60% estimate in the proposal headline, since it comes from a detailed analysis of the process.
Ask Claude to list more benefits of the redesign so the proposal looks fuller and harder for the director to dismiss.
Measure how long each onboarding step takes today, giving a real baseline to compare any improvement against.
Recommend replacing the whole process at once across every region, so the benefits arrive as soon as possible.
Propose a time-boxed trial with one team that tracks time saved and errors before any wider rollout is decided.

questions.explanation: Claude's 60% is an **estimate, not a measurement**. A sceptical director needs evidence: a **baseline** of today's step times (C) and a **small, measured trial** (E) that shows actual time saved and any errors. Together they turn a claim into data and limit the risk of the change.

whyWrong.A: Headlining an unmeasured estimate invites the exact scepticism she faces, and it overpromises if the trial lands lower.
whyWrong.B: Padding the list of benefits adds claims, not evidence. A sceptic will see it as advocacy.
whyWrong.D: A full rollout with no proof concentrates risk and gives the director a reason to say no.

questions.mindset: Turn AI estimates into measured evidence: baseline first, then a small pilot.

questions.stem: An IT procurement analyst uses Research to compare three document-management vendors. The cited report says Vendor B holds a particular security certification and offers a price that fits the budget, which together make B the recommendation. The shortlist goes to the security and finance teams on Friday. Which TWO checks are MOST important before sending it? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude how confident it is in each claim and keep any claim it rates at 90% confidence or above.
Confirm the security certification against the vendor's own published trust or compliance documentation.
Rerun the Research and keep only the claims that appear in both versions of the resulting report.
Confirm the pricing and its terms directly with the vendor, via a quote request or its official price page.
Make sure every sentence in the report carries a citation before the shortlist goes to security and finance.

questions.explanation: Verify **in proportion to the stakes**: check the claims the decision rests on. The certification (B) and the price (D) are what make Vendor B the pick, and both go to teams that will rely on them. Confirming them at the primary source catches stale pages, misread tiers or a citation that doesn't say what the report claims.

whyWrong.A: A self-rated confidence score isn't evidence; Claude can't confirm what its sources didn't say correctly.
whyWrong.C: Two runs can repeat the same outdated or misread source. Consistency isn't verification.
whyWrong.E: A citation shows where a claim came from, not that the source supports it. Full citation coverage still needs the key ones checked.

questions.mindset: Check the claims the decision depends on, at the primary source.

questions.stem: A service-desk manager uses Claude to map her team's ticket process and find bottlenecks. Claude's analysis is useful and identifies that agents spend about 20 minutes per incident re-entering details from the monitoring tool into the ticketing system. Claude suggests 'connecting the two systems so tickets are created automatically'. She has no coding background. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: Ask Claude to walk her through writing the integration code herself, so the improvement can go live quickly.
Paste the ticketing system's admin login into the chat so Claude can try to create the tickets directly.
Drop the suggestion because chat-based Claude can't connect systems, and focus only on other bottlenecks.
Write up the bottleneck, its time cost and the behavior wanted, and raise it with IT as a formal integration request.

questions.explanation: Claude's analysis did its job: it found a real bottleneck and sized it. Building a system-to-system integration is **technical work that Associates escalate** to Developers or Architects — it needs proper access controls and testing. Her best contribution is a clear request: what happens today, what it costs (20 minutes per incident) and what should happen instead.

whyWrong.A: An untested integration built by someone without coding experience risks broken tickets and security gaps. This belongs with IT.
whyWrong.B: Sharing admin credentials in chat breaks basic data-sensitivity practice, and chat isn't a sanctioned way to write into production systems.
whyWrong.C: The bottleneck is real and costly. Chat's limits are a reason to hand it to the right team, not to drop it.

questions.mindset: Use Claude to find and size the problem, then hand integration work to the people who build integrations.
